How is Connecticut organized when you sell a house?

Connecticut sells and taxes real estate through its towns, not its counties. The state has 169 municipalities: 19 cities, 149 towns and one borough. They are grouped into eight historical counties and nine planning regions, and the planning regions serve as the county equivalents. For a seller, that means the offices you deal with sit at town hall.

The assessor values the home, the tax collector sends the bill, and the town clerk records the deed. A house in Hamden is recorded in Hamden, even though the state still lists Hamden under New Haven County. We group our local guides below by historical county, but no county office will handle your paperwork.

If you want a starting point for your own town, our Connecticut guides by city and county collects the local pages in one place.

What do sellers owe in property tax and where do they pay it?

Property tax is a town matter, and the bill follows the October 1 grand list. Every town assesses at 70 percent of present true and actual value, so a home a buyer would pay $300,000 for shows an assessed value near $210,000. Towns revalue on a five-year cycle set by the Office of Policy and Management, which is why a whole neighborhood can jump in one year.

Appeals go to the town's board of assessment appeals, and the written filing deadline is in February. Unpaid tax turns delinquent after the first day of the following month and carries interest at 18 percent per year, with a $2 minimum. A town collector who levies on a house can run a tax sale, and the owner generally has up to six months after the sale to redeem. That window can drop to 60 days for abandoned property. Our Connecticut tax sale guide walks through the notices.

Older or disabled owners may qualify for the state circuit breaker credit, worth up to $1,000 for a single person and $1,250 for a married couple. Applications go to the local assessor between February 1 and May 15. Our property tax guide covers the rest, and the big cities have their own pages, such as Bridgeport, Hartford and Stamford.

What does it cost to transfer a Connecticut house?

The deed is recorded with the town clerk, and the seller pays the real estate conveyance tax when it is recorded. The tax applies when the consideration is $2,000 or more. For a house, the state portion is three-quarters of one percent of the price and the town portion is one-quarter of one percent. On a residential price of $800,000 or more, the state rate steps up on the part above $800,000. The seller or the seller's attorney files Form OP-236, and towns that take part in myCTREC accept it online.

Several transfers are exempt from the state tax. Transfers between spouses are one. A principal residence conveyed in lieu of foreclosure is another, as is a principal residence sold for too little to pay the mortgages and the priority tax and sewer liens. A home with a crumbling foundation caused by pyrrhotite can also qualify, but only for the first transfer after an engineer's written evaluation, and not for owners who received money from the Crumbling Foundations Assistance Fund. The municipal portion still applies to some of these, so ask the town clerk how your sale will be treated.

Recording itself is cheap. The statute sets $10 for the first page and $5 for each added page. Our quitclaim deed guide explains the formalities, including two witnesses and an acknowledgment.

How does foreclosure work in Connecticut?

Connecticut foreclosures go through the courts. A lender files suit, and the judge can order a strict foreclosure or, at the court's discretion, a sale by decree. A first mortgage can also be foreclosed by a market sale if the lender asks and the owner agrees. The statute does not give one fixed calendar for all cases, so the timeline depends on the court and on what the owner files. Ask a Connecticut attorney about your docket.

For residential mortgages where the case has a return date from July 1, 2009 through June 30, 2029, the lender must attach notice of the Ezequiel Santiago Foreclosure Mediation Program to the papers it serves on the owner. An owner who sells before the court acts may avoid a judgment, and the sale can happen at any point if the buyer can close fast.

  • Read every court paper and note the return date.
  • Ask the clerk about the mediation program and any deadline to file the certificate.
  • Get a payoff figure from the lender before comparing any sale offer.
  • Tell your attorney if a sale would leave a balance owed.

What happens to an inherited house in Connecticut?

Connecticut has 54 probate districts, and estates are handled in the Probate Court for the district where the decedent lived. The court appoints the executor or administrator, who can then deal with the house. Heirs often ask whether a Connecticut estate tax bill will stand in the way. For deaths in 2026 the exemption is $15 million, and no Connecticut estate or gift tax is due if the taxable estate is at or below that figure. The return is due six months after death unless extended.

Estate sales also get lighter paperwork on one point. Transfers made by executors, administrators, trustees or conservators are exempt from the residential condition report rule. Our estate and inheritance tax page explains what heirs owe, and the homestead page explains why the creditor shield of $250,000 under section 52-352b is not a tax break.

What must a seller disclose?

A person who offers residential property for sale must give the buyer a written residential condition report before the buyer signs a binder or contract. The buyer's signed receipt is attached to the offer. The statute lists exemptions, including transfers to a spouse, parent, sibling, child or grandparent with no consideration paid, newly built homes under an implied warranty, and transfers by fiduciaries.

Radon deserves a mention. The Department of Public Health recommends that residents throughout the state test their homes, and radon tests are often part of a real estate transaction. Testing is the only way to know the level. A short-term test runs 2 to 90 days, usually 2 to 7, and many local health departments hand out free or discounted kits.

  • Gather the report form early so a buyer can sign it before the contract.
  • Order a radon test if you have never run one.
  • Keep any engineer's letter about the foundation, since it matters for the tax exemption above.
  • Tell your buyer about repairs you will not make.

What if the house has tenants?

A buyer takes the landlord's duties with the building. Connecticut eviction is called summary process, and it starts with a Notice to Quit served by a state marshal that gives at least three full days before the case is filed. A tenant has a nine-day grace period on rent before a landlord can terminate for nonpayment. The security deposit is capped at two months' rent, or one month if the tenant is 62 or older, and whoever owns the house when the tenant moves out must return it, even if it was paid to the previous owner.

After a foreclosure, most bona fide tenants cannot be made to leave for at least 90 days after title passes, or until the lease ends if that is later. Our eviction guide and landlord and tenant guide go deeper.

What does a cash sale as-is mean in Connecticut?

In a cash sale as-is, the buyer pays without a mortgage and takes the house in its current condition. There is no lender appraisal to wait on, so the closing date is mostly a matter of title work and the town clerk's recording. The seller is still responsible for clear title, the tax and lien payoffs, and the conveyance tax owed at recording.

Cash Home Buyers works with Connecticut owners whose houses need repairs, carry back taxes, sit in probate or hold tenants. If you want to see how a cash purchase works, our Hartford, New Haven and Bridgeport pages explain the process for those towns.

Who to call depends on the question. The town assessor answers value, the tax collector answers what is owed, the town clerk answers recording and conveyance tax, and the Probate Court answers estate questions. A Connecticut attorney should review anything that involves a court case.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Connecticut have?

Connecticut has eight historical counties and nine planning regions, but towns do the real work. There are 169 municipalities, and each assesses, bills and records on its own.

Who do I pay property tax to?

You pay your town's tax collector. The assessor sets the value at 70 percent of true value as of October 1, and unpaid bills accrue 18 percent annual interest.

What is the conveyance tax when I sell?

On a home, the state charges 0.75 percent of the price and the town charges 0.25 percent. The state rate rises on the part of a residential price above $800,000.

Is foreclosure judicial in Connecticut?

Yes. The court can order a strict foreclosure or a sale by decree. Eligible residential cases must also be offered the foreclosure mediation program.

Do I need a condition report to sell?

Usually yes. You must give the buyer a written residential condition report before the buyer signs. Fiduciary transfers, such as by an executor, are exempt.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate ends?

The executor or administrator appointed by the Probate Court handles the sale. Connecticut has 54 probate districts, so call the court for your decedent's district.

Does a tenant have to move out when I sell?

Not automatically. A buyer takes the landlord's duties, and after foreclosure most bona fide tenants get at least 90 days. A lease may last longer.
